Ask HN: Are the trades a safe career transition?

56 points by Rd6n6 20 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 94 comments

I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged

I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement...

Are the trades safe?

Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off

Grombobulous 18 hours ago | next [–]

If you look at a graph of the US economy, and remove software and data centers, there’s basically no growth.

Don’t leave software. AI will change your job, but it won’t replace you, not even in multiple decades.

Be strategic about the kinds of software roles you get into. Look for niches with stability. Look to go toward highly regulated software niches. For example, I work in an area where it would be impossible to remove manual testers due to certain regulations.

Software work for government where you must be a US citizen or you must do specific things manually could be another example.

I also think some areas are going to be more insulated from AI disruption. I think ops and security have more stability. Anything that requires more judgment and less “take inputs and turn them into outputs.”

Moving from an upper middle class career track to something you can get into without a high school diploma is a mistake. In many trades you’re competing with dudes who are working under the table and aren’t even documented. Even if you’re not, they’re mostly hard on your body, and some aren’t even immune from automation.

Software is still on the high end of the spectrum of career cushiness, it's just no longer a full on outlier. If you've already put a decade or more into this career track, switching to another career will have you starting at the bottom of a ladder that is significantly more rigid and inflexible than you remember the early years of your career being, with higher-run perks still no better than what we have here now.

Better to make the lateral move from 2010s-software-eng to post-AI-software-eng than to start from scratch at the bottom of an equal or worse ladder.

AI is definitely changing things a lot in the field, but don't discount the massive change in how cheap money was during ZIRP and how expensive it became after ZIRP finally ended. This was coincidentally around the same time the layoffs in big tech started, which was before AI really had any meaningful impact. When money is cheap it is a lot easier for companies to hire, and when money suddenly stops being cheap it is a lot harder.

In particular, large discontinuities in economic conditions, which we just experienced recently post-covid, always produce downturns in affected industries (which is distinct from the first order aspect of how expensive money is). So I think even ignoring AI we could expect several years of down-ness and reorganization followed by a recovery.

I don't think we can even tell this point if AI will reduce demand for developers. The economy for software might be even worse right now if the AI developments hadn't happened when they did, there was an insane hiring spree during COVID and even before that the industry employment-side was growing at a probably unsustainable pace.

I'm flabbergasted that people are not seeing the danger here. If you count back-to-back tax for a real employee vs a virtual employee (not that I seriously claim GPUs are that far along yet). Governments are making employees A LOT more expensive at the exact time private companies are bringing (for now limited versions of) virtual employees on the market.

Back to back tax is ... let's say I own a company and make pencils. You love pencils, and so you work for me. I pay you 100k (to make calculation easier), and you have a love of pencils that might even be called unhealthy. So every cent I pay you, you use to buy pencils from me. I put that money in my personal back account, according to normal correct procedure (ie. paying company tax, dividend tax, ...). I like to claim this is a better measure of 2 tax rates: personal tax, and "1-round-trip-through-people-in-the-economy" tax. How much do I get on my (personal) bank account? In the US: about 38k. In France? 21k. In most of Europe it'll be maybe 31k.

We are effectively taxing productive labor at 62%. France is effectively taxing labor at 79%, Europe at about 70%, and that's the rate in Germany too. This is ignoring things like the maximum hours regulation in France, which effectively further increases taxes, not per person, but per "person-hour" of labor. Of course the key thing to realize in Europe is that the tax on imported products ... is only 15% or so, less than a third (now this is because many products people depend on have moved to imports, from the grain people bake with to iphones. So people will very directly feel tax increases there). This is also why any industry that needs people is moving, for instance French chocolate is now really either Swiss or Indian.

These taxes are being raised further now.

So now that jobs are under threat from being taken over by AI, the government is raising taxes on labor, making sure the price difference between a real employee and a virtual employee, already a factor 2-3, is rising close to a factor 4.

Cue the screams everywhere (especially in Germany) about companies not wanting to hire people ... while government is making it harder and harder to hire people ... at the exact time the first semi-semi-viable replacement for people is coming on the market.

Product prices are going to be defined by how much AI can make them. The more humans involved the more expensive they'll be. And this is very much a policy choice, NOT companies or monopolies or tech bros or ... doing it (they'll be profiting since social media are THE example of an AI produced good/service)

So once again business owners will be astonished, while doing layoffs, asking "if this isn't what you want, why are democratic governments pushing this so hard?".

Something to keep in mind in these kind of discussions: the most pessimistic visions of the future are not worth preparing for on an individual level even if they end up materializing. This is because apocalyptic problems can only be reasonably addressed with solutions that are very large-scale and political in nature, and trying to minimise your own personal exposure is akin to doomsday prepping.

If the doomers are right and AI fully automates knowledge work leaving most unable to produce much value, the entire notion of a 'safe career path' doesn’t make sense. Not just because of robotics, but also because demand for even the safest bets likely collapses in such a scenario. And honestly, in this case there would be far more pressing issues than long term job security.

IMO, make decisions like these based on what fulfils you rather than out of fear.

Many responses will be straw dogs about trades are universally all physically disabling. If you're a crane operator and you're trying to lift 175 tons with your own knees and back, you're doing it wrong. Its easy to find trades jobs in almost any environment. There are physically punishing jobs like roofer or concrete work, but that does not somehow prove all the other jobs are debilitating.

Many people die young and fat and very sick at desk jobs. Inertness does not seem to equal health. A job like industrial maint electrician involves just enough walking around to outlive the average desk jockey. Of course there are very fat and sick heavy equipment operators...

Another meme response you'll get implies its all your choice to "stay in" whereas the problem is the market is contracting so fast you won't be allowed in if you're not already in, and if you're kicked out (layoff, just not keeping on the official mandatory career path, etc) you'll never ever get back in. Don't worry about deciding to leave software development, plan ahead for when you're uncontrollably permanently kicked out. Its not going to be your decision.

Education can be helpful on the jobsite. I've seen fine finish woodworkers do very weird, yet successful, graphical solutions to avoid five seconds of trigonometry. Automation PLC programmers will do weird stuff to avoid bode plots and similar control theory topics. There are people tuning PID controllers on the job who don't know or understand the P, I or D, they just twiddle the knobs until it works right, often while developing all sorts of magical mythology.

Keep in mind the wide spectrum of the size of your counterparty. Working for a multinational megacorporation at a mine operating heavy equipment for your entire career will be wildly different experience from working for a single human individual digging a septic field for a day.

An interesting analogy with lawyers is people like to think their interface is like a chatbot so a chatbot will replace them. But people actually HIRE lawyers because they want to outsource the risks of doing something legal-related to someone else, in a way its an insurance gig not a chatbot gig. You'll find in the trades they're not really hiring a guy to move the levers to dig a trench, they're outsourcing the risk and hassle of owning your own excavator machine and the risks of screwed up one-call utility marking, etc. In a similar way a robot arm that can screw a wire to a wall switch won't replace an electrician who knows how to run wires without taking an axe to every piece of plaster in the room. Its fascinating how the invention of CNC machines has not resulted in machine shops closing down and every company broom closet having their own personal robot mill and lathe, but it has changed the entire experience of working at a machine shop... See also 3d printing LOL.
